chunks: From him, from al-Hajjaj, from Ubayd ibn Ishaq, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I am an owner of date palms; inform me of a limit to which I should adhere regarding fulfillment (of obligations).' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Intend fulfillment; if it comes to your hands and you have intended fulfillment, you will be among the people of fulfillment. And if you intended deficiency, then fulfilled, you will be among the people of deficiency.'

key_terms.صَاحِبُ نَخْلٍ: Owner of date palms (referring to agricultural tax/obligations)

ai.seo_question: How does intention affect the spiritual value of fulfilling financial or religious obligations in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that *niyyah* (intention) determines the spiritual quality of an act, not merely its external completion. It illustrates that even if one fulfills the literal requirement of paying the crop due share, a heart inclined toward deficiency renders the act one of the deficient, whereas a sincere intent to fully honor the obligation secures the status of the faithful fulfillers. This underscores the importance of internal sincerity in commercial transactions and agricultural dues.
